stops.name: Rosario: Entre Ríos 480, birthplace
stops.campa: In a rented apartment on Calle Entre Ríos, Ernesto Guevara de la Serna is born to Ernesto Guevara Lynch and Celia de la Serna, aristocrats of restless blood: Irish rebels and Spanish viceroys in the line. The family is only passing through Rosario, bound downriver; the child of the journey is born mid-journey. His father will say later that in his son's veins flowed the blood of Irish rebels, and that Ernesto was born with it already in revolt. The storm of the century's second half enters the world quietly, wrapped against the river damp.

sources: Jon Lee Anderson, Che Guevara: A Revolutionary Life

stops.name: Caraguataí, Misiones, the yerba mate plantation
stops.campa: The family lives on the wild bank of the Alto Paraná, where the father plants yerba mate and the jungle presses in: snakes, red earth, the river running like a green god past the landing. The infant Ernesto is carried through plantations where mensú laborers work off debts they can never pay; his mother swims the dangerous river while he watches from the bank. The first landscape of his life is the frontier itself: heat, insects, the poor bent over the bitter leaf that Argentina drinks.
suggested_refs: Photographs of the Guevara family at Puerto Caraguataí, c. 1929-1930
sources: Ernesto Guevara Lynch, Mi hijo el Che
Jon Lee Anderson, Che Guevara: A Revolutionary Life

stops.name: San Isidro, Buenos Aires, the first asthma attack
stops.campa: On the second of May his mother takes the two-year-old swimming at the club on a cold autumn morning, and that night the child begins to drown in air. The asthma arrives like a lifelong angel of contradiction: the disease that will chain him to inhalers and cortisone is the same one that forges the will of iron. The doctors say the boy may not live a normal life. The family begins its wandering in search of breathable air, and the boy begins his apprenticeship in fighting his own body every single night.
suggested_refs: Guevara Lynch's account of the May 1930 swimming outing in Mi hijo el Che
sources: Ernesto Guevara Lynch, Mi hijo el Che
Jon Lee Anderson, Che Guevara: A Revolutionary Life

stops.name: Alta Gracia, Córdoba, Villa Nydia
stops.campa: For the boy's lungs the family climbs to the dry hill air of Alta Gracia and settles at Villa Nydia. Here the legend of the sickly child who refuses to be sick is written: between attacks he cannot walk to school, so Celia teaches him to read in bed among her books; between books he hurls himself at football, golf, and fistfights with the sons of quarry workers and caddies, the poor boys he prefers. Spanish Republican exiles pass through the parlor with the smell of a lost war. The asthma dictates the rhythm; the will dictates everything else.
suggested_refs: Villa Nydia, today the Museo Casa del Che, Alta Gracia
Childhood photograph of Ernesto with the Granado brothers' circle in Córdoba
sources: Ernesto Guevara Lynch, Mi hijo el Che
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Che_Guevara

stops.name: Córdoba, Colegio Deán Funes, meeting Alberto Granado
stops.campa: The family moves down to Córdoba city and Ernesto enters the Deán Funes secondary school. On the rugby pitch of Estudiantes he throws his wheezing body into the scrum, pausing at the touchline for his inhaler, and earns the name Fuser: Furibundo Serna, the furious one. The team's trainer is a short, laughing biochemistry student named Alberto Granado, six years older, keeper of a motorcycle and of large ideas. The friendship that will drive across a continent is founded here, between scrums, over books by Freud, Neruda and Verne.
suggested_refs: Team photograph of the Estudiantes rugby side, Córdoba, mid-1940s
sources: Alberto Granado, Traveling with Che Guevara
Jon Lee Anderson, Che Guevara: A Revolutionary Life

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Faculty of Medicine
stops.campa: Celia's cancer and the family's move bring Ernesto to Buenos Aires, where he enrolls in medicine at the university on Calle Paraguay. He works in Dr. Pisani's allergy clinic, hunting his own disease down the microscope, half-patient and half-researcher. He reads omnivorously, plays chess, keeps a handwritten philosophical dictionary, and takes jobs and journeys whenever the city grows too small. The examiners know him as brilliant and absent by turns; the road already has more authority over him than the lecture hall.
stops.quote: When I began to study medicine... I dreamed of becoming a famous researcher, of working tirelessly to achieve something that could truly be placed at the disposal of humanity.
stops.quote_source: Ernesto Che Guevara, speech 'On Revolutionary Medicine', Havana, 19 August 1960 (recalling his student years)
suggested_refs: Student record of Ernesto Guevara de la Serna, Facultad de Ciencias Médicas, Universidad de Buenos Aires
sources: Che Guevara, On Revolutionary Medicine (1960)
Jon Lee Anderson, Che Guevara: A Revolutionary Life

stops.name: San Francisco del Chañar: the leprosarium, on the motorized bicycle
stops.campa: On the first of January 1950 the medical student pedals out of Buenos Aires alone on a bicycle fitted with a tiny Cucciolo motor, bound for the north, four thousand five hundred kilometers through twelve provinces. He climbs to the leprosarium of San Francisco del Chañar where Alberto Granado now works, and for the first time sits long hours with lepers, learning that the sick want a hand shaken without gloves more than they want pity. The manufacturer of the little motor will run his photograph as an advertisement: the first published image of the traveler.
suggested_refs: Micrón motor advertisement featuring Guevara's testimonial letter and photo with the motorized bicycle, 1950
sources: Alberto Granado, Traveling with Che Guevara
https://www.armenianexplorer.com/article/che-guevara's-first-journey-on-a-motorized-bicycle

stops.name: Salta, the hospital and the soul of a people
stops.campa: At the northern apex of the ride he sleeps in police stations and hospital corridors, taking Argentina in through the skin: cane cutters of Tucumán, the dispossessed of the dry Chaco edge, vagabonds who share fire and mate. In Salta the hospital staff ask the returning cyclist what he has seen, and he understands that he has not traveled the way tourists travel. He writes it down in the notebook, the first formulation of the creed: the country is read in its sick, its prisoners, its anxious passersby, not in its monuments.
stops.quote: I am not nourished by the same things as tourists... the soul of a people is reflected in the sick of its hospitals, the inmates of its police stations, the anxious passerby one talks to.
stops.quote_source: Ernesto Guevara, 1950 travel notebook, cited in Anderson's biography
suggested_refs: Pages of the 1950 bicycle-trip notebook
sources: Jon Lee Anderson, Che Guevara: A Revolutionary Life
http://timelinesandsoundtracks.blogspot.com/2020/11/che-guevara-timeline.html

stops.name: Buenos Aires, departure on La Poderosa II
stops.campa: On the fourth of January, Ernesto, twenty-three, and Alberto Granado, twenty-nine, roar out of Buenos Aires on La Poderosa II, Alberto's overloaded 1939 Norton 500: the Mighty One, named with irony and love. The plan is continental and absurd: the whole spine of Latin America, ending at a leprosarium on the Amazon. Celia weeps at the departure. The bike carries a tent, a revolver, a grill, and two futures. Nine symbolic months of gestation begin; what will be born at the end is not the same young man who leaves.
stops.quote: This is not a story of heroic feats... it is a glimpse of two lives running parallel for a time, with similar hopes and convergent dreams.
stops.quote_source: Ernesto Che Guevara, The Motorcycle Diaries, preface ('So we understand each other')
suggested_refs: Photograph of Ernesto and Alberto astride La Poderosa II before departure
sources: Che Guevara, The Motorcycle Diaries
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Motorcycle_Diaries_(book)

stops.name: Miramar, Chichina by the sea
stops.campa: The road bends first toward love. At the resort of Miramar, María del Carmen 'Chichina' Ferreyra, heiress of Córdoba aristocracy, summers with her disapproving family, and two planned days stretch to eight. Ernesto carries her gift, a gold bracelet as amulet, and leaves her his dog, ominously named Comeback. On the dunes the two futures pull against each other: the estancia and the road. The sea witnesses the wager. When La Poderosa finally points south again, something has already been decided that neither of them says aloud.
suggested_refs: Photograph of Chichina Ferreyra, c. 1951
The chapter 'Lost horizons' in the Motorcycle Diaries manuscript

stops.name: Bahía Blanca, last city of the pampa
stops.campa: The travelers rest with friends in Bahía Blanca, the last big town before the desert of the south, patching the Norton and their finances. Leaving, Ernesto rides feverish and half-delirious into the dunes of Médanos, where the heavy bike bucks and falls again and again in the loose sand; he counts the spills like a boxer counting knockdowns. Fever forces him into bed. The journey is teaching its first lesson: the continent is not scenery, it is an adversary, and it will be crossed on its own terms.
suggested_refs: Motorcycle Diaries chapter recounting the nine falls in the sand at Médanos
sources: Che Guevara, The Motorcycle Diaries

stops.name: Choele Choel, fever in the Río Negro valley
stops.campa: Burning with flu, Ernesto is carried to the small regional hospital at Choele Choel on the Río Negro, where penicillin and days of sleep pull him back. Alberto charms the doctors; the patient, restless, writes. In the irrigated valley the two future leprologists are treated as colleagues, given beds and meals in exchange for medical talk. It is the journey's rhythm now: break down, be rescued by the kindness of ordinary Argentines, repay in stories, roll on. The Norton waits outside like a tethered animal.
suggested_refs: The regional hospital of Choele Choel, where Guevara recovered
sources: Che Guevara, The Motorcycle Diaries
Alberto Granado, Traveling with Che Guevara

stops.name: San Martín de los Andes, Lake Lácar and the vocation
stops.campa: The road climbs into the lake country and stops the travelers' breath: Lácar lying dark blue between forested walls, the Andes closing the sky. They camp, roast stolen-cheap lamb, and are offered a future: a local caretaker's dream of a clinic on the lakeshore, a settled life in paradise. That night by the water both men look at the offered happiness and refuse it, and in the refusal discover what they actually are. The diary records the vow of the wanderers; the lake keeps the oath.
stops.quote: Then we understood that our vocation, our true vocation, was to roam forever along the roads and seas of the world.
stops.quote_source: Ernesto Che Guevara, The Motorcycle Diaries
suggested_refs: Lake Lácar shoreline at San Martín de los Andes; plaque commemorating the 1952 passage
sources: Che Guevara, The Motorcycle Diaries

stops.name: San Carlos de Bariloche, Chichina's letter
stops.campa: Along the Seven Lakes road the Norton limps into Bariloche, and in the poste restante a letter from Chichina waits like a document of severance: it is over. Ernesto reads it in the shelter's kitchen light and something closes quietly. He had carried her bracelet as an amulet; now the last anchor to the life of the Córdoba salons is cut by the woman herself. The diary is laconic and wounded. Outside, Nahuel Huapi lies under storm light, and across the water is Chile: the road forward, which is now the only direction he owns.
suggested_refs: Motorcycle Diaries chapter on reading Chichina's farewell letter in Bariloche
sources: Che Guevara, The Motorcycle Diaries

stops.name: Lakes crossing to Peulla, into Chile over Frías
stops.campa: The frontier is crossed by water, in the old ceremonial way: the Modesta Victoria across Nahuel Huapi, the green mirror of Laguna Frías, La Poderosa lashed to the deck like a sarcophagus, and finally Peulla on the Chilean side, under the white cone of Tronador. Customs men eye the overloaded bike and the two threadbare 'doctors'. Argentina drops behind with Chichina's letter still fresh; Chile opens ahead as the first foreign country of the myth, lake-cold and volcano-lit. The continent begins here.
suggested_refs: The lake steamer route Nahuel Huapi–Frías–Peulla, still operating as the Cruce Andino
sources: Che Guevara, The Motorcycle Diaries
Alberto Granado, Traveling with Che Guevara

stops.name: Temuco, 'two Argentine experts in leprology'
stops.campa: In Temuco the travelers perform their masterpiece of picaresque diplomacy: the newspaper El Austral publishes them under the headline 'Two Argentine experts in leprology travel South America by motorcycle,' and for a week the clipping is a passport that opens garages, dinner tables and wine cellars. Ernesto notes with amusement how a little printed importance transforms them from vagabonds into dignitaries. The Norton, less impressed by fame, is coming apart beneath them, shedding pieces of itself along the Chilean south.
suggested_refs: El Austral de Temuco article, 19 February 1952: 'Dos expertos argentinos en leprología recorren Sudamérica en motocicleta'
sources: Che Guevara, The Motorcycle Diaries
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Motorcycle_Diaries_(book)

stops.name: Lautaro, the dance, the chase, the dying Norton
stops.campa: At Lautaro the gearbox is welded and the town offers a dance. Ernesto, loose with Chilean wine, courts a mechanic's wife too openly on the dance floor and the evening ends with the two Argentines fleeing the hall under a hail of curses, pursued by indignant husbands and their friends. Days later, on the road toward Malleco, La Poderosa's frame gives way at last in a slow, terminal crash. The Mighty One's agony has begun: from here the motorcycle journey becomes a journey of walkers, stowaways and beggars, which is to say, its true self.
suggested_refs: Motorcycle Diaries chapter on the Lautaro dance and the breakdown
sources: Che Guevara, The Motorcycle Diaries
Alberto Granado, Traveling with Che Guevara

stops.name: Los Ángeles, death of La Poderosa
stops.campa: In Los Ángeles the verdict is pronounced: La Poderosa II will ride no more. The travelers sleep in the fire station among the volunteer firemen, and Ernesto joins a midnight run to a burning house, hauling hose in borrowed helmet: the asthmatic medical student as bombero for one night. The dead Norton is crated onto a truck for Santiago. Stripped of their machine, the two are now purely what the road makes them: cargo, guests, mendicants of Latin America. The diary notes the loss like the death of a comrade.
suggested_refs: The Los Ángeles volunteer fire company where the travelers lodged, February 1952
sources: Che Guevara, The Motorcycle Diaries
Alberto Granado, Traveling with Che Guevara

stops.name: Santiago de Chile, farewell to the machine
stops.campa: Santiago receives them on the back of the truck that carries the corpse of La Poderosa. In the capital they leave the motorcycle in a garage forever, gate-crash the hospitality of the Argentine consulate, and study the political fever of election-year Chile: Ibáñez posters, Allende posters, talk in every kitchen. Ernesto diagnoses the country in his notebook with the cold, affectionate eye that is becoming his instrument. Then, with nothing left to ride, the two point themselves north toward the desert on foot and by grace of passing trucks.
suggested_refs: Motorcycle Diaries chapter 'La Gioconda's smile' and notes on Chilean politics, 1952
sources: Che Guevara, The Motorcycle Diaries

stops.name: Valparaíso, La Gioconda and the dying woman
stops.campa: In the vertical port city, all stairways and funiculars and ship smoke, the owner of the café La Gioconda feeds the penniless travelers on credit and philosophy. Ernesto is called to a shack on the hills to see an old woman dying of asthma and heart failure amid poverty with nothing to prescribe. Standing uselessly at her bed, the young doctor has the vision that reorders his life: medicine cannot cure what an unjust order inflicts. The diary entry he writes that night is the first page of the revolutionary he will become.
stops.quote: There, in the final moments of people whose farthest horizon has always been tomorrow, one grasps the profound tragedy that circumscribes the life of the proletariat the whole world over.
stops.quote_source: Ernesto Che Guevara, The Motorcycle Diaries, Valparaíso chapter

stops.name: Stowaways on the San Antonio: Valparaíso to Antofagasta
stops.campa: Denied passage to Easter Island and short of everything, the two smuggle themselves aboard the freighter San Antonio in the night, hiding in a latrine among the smell of the sea's injustice. Discovered at sea, they are hauled before an amused captain and sentenced to work: Alberto peels potatoes, Ernesto scrubs the famous latrine. On deck at night, wind over the black Pacific, the stowaway watches the coast of the great desert north slide by and feels the joy of the trick: the continent crossed by cunning when money fails.
suggested_refs: The freighter San Antonio; Motorcycle Diaries chapter 'This time, disaster'
sources: Che Guevara, The Motorcycle Diaries
Alberto Granado, Traveling with Che Guevara

stops.name: Baquedano, the communist couple in the desert night
stops.campa: In the freezing dark of the Atacama, at the rail junction of Baquedano, the travelers share a candle and a blanketless night with a mining couple: communists, hounded, the man just out of prison, both walking toward the sulphur mines where no one asks your politics because the work kills you regardless. They have not one blanket between them. Ernesto gives them his and lies awake in the cold. In the couple's silent dignity he sees, he writes, the living portrait of the proletariat of the whole world, and the night enters the canon as a conversion scene.
stops.quote: It was one of the coldest nights of my life, but one which made me feel a little closer to this strange, for me, human species.
stops.quote_source: Ernesto Che Guevara, The Motorcycle Diaries, Baquedano chapter

stops.name: Chuquicamata, the copper mountain
stops.campa: They stand at the lip of the largest open-pit copper mine on earth, an amphitheater of terraces gnawed into the Andes by American machinery, and watch the wealth of Chile ride conveyor belts toward other people's futures. The blond, efficient managers of the Yankee company tolerate the visitors without warmth; the miners' graveyard tolerates everyone. Ernesto counts the dead in silicosis and the profit in dollars and writes the arithmetic into his notebook. Chuquicamata is the journey's great industrial vision: the mountain eaten alive, and the verdict forming.
stops.quote: The greatest effort Chile must make is to shake its uncomfortable Yankee friend from its back.
stops.quote_source: Ernesto Che Guevara, The Motorcycle Diaries, Chuquicamata chapter

stops.name: Tarata, the defeated race
stops.campa: Crossing into Peru at Tacna and climbing by truck into the altiplano, the travelers reach the stone village of Tarata, where Aymara families ride the truck-beds with their animals and their silence. Ernesto looks at faces that once belonged to an empire and sees four centuries of defeat administered like a slow medicine. The diary entry he writes here is the harshest and most pitying of the journey: the Indian world is not picturesque to him, it is a crime scene. The mountains hold the cold; the notebook holds the indictment.
stops.quote: The people before us are not the same proud race that time and again rose up against Inca rule... these are a defeated race.
stops.quote_source: Ernesto Che Guevara, The Motorcycle Diaries, Tarata chapter
suggested_refs: Motorcycle Diaries chapter on the truck ride through Tarata and the altiplano
sources: Che Guevara, The Motorcycle Diaries

stops.name: Cuzco, the navel of the world
stops.campa: In Cuzco the travelers walk on three cities at once: the Inca wall, the conquistador church built upon it, and the poor town breathing around both. Ernesto haunts the museum and the fortress of Sacsayhuamán, reads chronicles in the library, and lets the stones argue with him about empire and defeat. He writes that no other word fits the city: everything here summons what was, and accuses what is. The asthmatic Argentine on the temple steps is being conscripted, monument by monument, into the memory of the continent.
stops.quote: Cuzco: the one word that defines it exactly is evocation.
stops.quote_source: Ernesto Che Guevara, The Motorcycle Diaries, Cuzco chapters
suggested_refs: The twelve-angled stone and Inca walls of Calle Hatunrumiyoc, Cuzco
sources: Che Guevara, The Motorcycle Diaries

stops.name: Machu Picchu, the stone enigma
stops.campa: They climb to the dead city hanging between peaks and cloud, and for once the diary drops its irony. Ernesto and Alberto have the ruins nearly to themselves; they play football on the sacred plaza with a borrowed ball, drink mate against the cold, and talk half-seriously of revolution in America while the Urubamba roars far below. Machu Picchu enters him as proof: a native civilization whole, powerful, and murdered incomplete. He will write it up as an essay. The tourist comes to rest; he has come to read a verdict in stone.
stops.quote: Here is the pure expression of the most powerful indigenous civilization in the Americas, untouched by contact with the conquering armies.
stops.quote_source: Ernesto Guevara, 'Machu-Picchu, enigma de piedra en América', published in Siete, Panama, December 1953
suggested_refs: Photograph of Ernesto and Alberto seated at Machu Picchu, April 1952
sources: Che Guevara, The Motorcycle Diaries

stops.name: Huancarama and the Huambo leprosarium
stops.campa: Through rain and mud, on horses requisitioned from unwilling peasants and consciences uneasy about it, the travelers ride to the leper station of Huambo above Huancarama: a poor scatter of huts where the sick live almost without medicine, attended by devotion alone. Ernesto's asthma breaks him here; he lies for days in a peasant house, injecting himself with adrenaline, feverish among the mountains. The visit is short and the lesson long: this is what leprosy looks like when the patients are Indians and the state has looked away.

sources: Che Guevara, The Motorcycle Diaries

stops.name: Lima, Dr. Hugo Pesce, the master
stops.campa: In Lima the travelers are taken in by Dr. Hugo Pesce, leprologist, Marxist, disciple of Mariátegui, who feeds them every evening and talks science, socialism and Peru deep into the night. At the Hospital de Guía Ernesto works with the lepers, who love him because he refuses gloves and shakes their hands; when the two leave, the patients collect money and buy them a stove. Pesce is the journey's secret professor: in his clinic the two vocations, medicine and revolution, are shown to be one discipline.
stops.quote: To Doctor Hugo Pesce: who provoked, perhaps without knowing it, a great change in my attitude toward life and society.
stops.quote_source: Handwritten dedication by Che Guevara in a copy of La guerra de guerrillas sent to Pesce, 1960

stops.name: Iquitos, down the Ucayali on La Cenepa
stops.campa: From Pucallpa they ride the river highway of the Amazon aboard the boat La Cenepa, hammocks slung among traders, soldiers and pigs, Ernesto flattened by asthma attacks and reading in the wet heat. Iquitos receives them, the rubber-boom city marooned in jungle, reachable by no road on earth, and the hospital lends them beds and insecticide while they wait for passage. Here the map runs out of lines; from Iquitos onward the only geography is the brown river itself, moving toward the leper colony that has been the journey's destination from the first day.
suggested_refs: The river launch El Cisne/La Cenepa route Pucallpa–Iquitos, 1952
sources: Che Guevara, The Motorcycle Diaries

stops.name: San Pablo leper colony, the birthday toast
stops.campa: At the leprosarium of San Pablo, six hundred patients live on the far bank of the Amazon from their doctors. Ernesto and Alberto cross the water daily without gloves, hunt, fish, play football with the sick and treat them as men, and the colony returns to them a fierce love. On the night of the fourteenth of June, his twenty-fourth birthday, the staff throw a party, and Ernesto, pisco-warmed, stands and gives the toast the canon keeps: America is one mestizo nation from Mexico to the Strait. Days later he swims the whole width of the Amazon to the patients' side.
stops.quote: We constitute a single mestizo race with remarkable ethnographic similarities from Mexico to the Magellan Straits. And so, in an attempt to rid myself of the weight of small-minded provincialism, I propose a toast to Peru and to a United Latin America.
stops.quote_source: Ernesto Che Guevara, The Motorcycle Diaries, 'Saint Guevara's Day', San Pablo, 14 June 1952
suggested_refs: Photograph of Guevara and Granado with patients and staff at San Pablo, June 1952
sources: Che Guevara, The Motorcycle Diaries

stops.name: The Amazon, raft Mambo-Tango
stops.campa: The patients and staff of San Pablo build the travelers a raft with a roof and a name: Mambo-Tango, Cuba's rhythm lashed to Argentina's, and the colony's boats escort them into the current with songs. For two days the raft drifts the immense brown river: fishing lines, rain, chess with the mosquitoes, the jungle sliding past like time itself. In the dark they overshoot Leticia entirely and wake in Brazilian waters, their chicken lost to the river, their dignity bartered to a fisherman to be hauled back upstream. The Amazon has stamped the passports.

sources: Che Guevara, The Motorcycle Diaries

stops.name: Leticia, football coaches of the Colombian Amazon
stops.campa: Stranded and centavo-less in the Colombian river port of Leticia, the two Argentines convert their nationality into a trade: any countryman of Di Stéfano must know football. Hired to train the local team, Ernesto keeps goal, asthma permitting, while Alberto drills the forwards, and the team rises gloriously in the local tournament. The town pays them in beds, meals and half-fare air tickets. It is picaresque scripture: the future comandante's first command in Colombia is a football squad in the deepest jungle.
suggested_refs: The Leticia football tournament of June-July 1952 in Granado's memoir
sources: Alberto Granado, Traveling with Che Guevara

stops.name: Bogotá, the suffocated city
stops.campa: A military cargo plane lifts them out of the jungle to Bogotá, a capital under the leaden peace of La Violencia, four years after the Bogotazo burned it. Soldiers on the corners, rifles and tear gas, the dictatorship of Laureano Gómez pressing on every conversation. Ernesto's dagger, drawn to sketch a map in the dirt, brings the police down on him; the travelers are advised urgently to love Colombia from farther away. In the letter to his mother written here he takes the country's blood pressure and finds it strangling.
stops.quote: There is more repression of individual freedom here than in any country we've been to; the police patrol the streets carrying rifles and demand your papers every few minutes... the atmosphere is tense and it seems a revolution may be brewing.
stops.quote_source: Letter from Ernesto Guevara to his mother, Bogotá, 6 July 1952
suggested_refs: Letter to Celia de la Serna from Bogotá, 6 July 1952
sources: Che Guevara, The Motorcycle Diaries (appended letters)
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Motorcycle_Diaries_(book)

stops.name: Caracas, the parting of the two travelers
stops.campa: By bus over the Andes and down to the hot Caribbean bowl of Caracas, the journey arrives at its own ending. Alberto takes work at the leprosarium of Cabo Blanco and stays; Ernesto must return to Buenos Aires to finish medicine, one exam-year left. In the hillside barrios he walks among the poverty that ringed the oil boom, writing hard sentences. The two friends part with a promise to meet again on the road: a promise the century will keep in its own way. La Poderosa's crew is dissolved; the diarist travels on alone.

Alberto Granado, Traveling with Che Guevara

stops.name: Buenos Aires, return, and the note in the margin
stops.campa: He flies home the long way: aboard a cargo plane hauling racehorses via Miami, where a delayed engine strands him a month, hungry, in the belly of the empire itself. Back in Buenos Aires he sits the last exams in a fury of study and qualifies as doctor. But the diary closes with a prophecy set down as plain fact: the traveler who returned is not the one who left. In the famous note in the margin he declares which half of humanity he will stand with when the dividing wind blows, and offers himself for the sacrifice in advance.
stops.quote: I knew that when the great guiding spirit cleaves humanity into two antagonistic halves, I will be with the people... I feel my nostrils dilate, savoring the acrid smell of gunpowder and blood, of the enemy's death.
stops.quote_source: Ernesto Che Guevara, The Motorcycle Diaries, final chapter ('A note in the margin')
suggested_refs: Manuscript of 'A note in the margin'

segments.name: Soldier of America: The Second Journey

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Retiro station, the second departure
stops.campa: Doctor now, and determined never to practice quietly, Ernesto boards the Belgrano railway at Retiro with his childhood friend Calica Ferrer, second-class to Bolivia, fleeing both military service and the settled life. On the platform stand Celia and the whole clan. As the train pulls out he leans from the window and shouts the sentence the family will repeat forever, announcing not a trip but an enlistment. He does not know it, but he is leaving Argentina for good: the country will next receive him as ashes of a legend.
stops.quote: ¡Aquí va un soldado de América! — Here goes a soldier of America!
stops.quote_source: Guevara's shout from the departing train at Retiro, 7 July 1953, recorded in family memoirs (Guevara Lynch; Calica Ferrer, De Ernesto al Che)
suggested_refs: Retiro railway station platform, Buenos Aires

sources: Carlos 'Calica' Ferrer, De Ernesto al Che
Jon Lee Anderson, Che Guevara: A Revolutionary Life

stops.name: La Paz, the revolution observed
stops.campa: The train climbs into the Bolivian altiplano and drops the travelers into a city boiling with the aftermath of the 1952 revolution: miners with slung rifles in the streets, the MNR handing out land and votes, Indian peasants entering ministries that had never let them past the door. Ernesto watches with the skeptic's eye. He sees the DDT sprayed on peasants in the ministry waiting room and pronounces the revolution incomplete. In the diary of this second journey La Paz appears as a splendid, turbulent lesson in what half-revolutions look like.
stops.quote: La Paz is the Shanghai of the Americas.
stops.quote_source: Ernesto Guevara, diary of the second journey (Otra vez / Back on the Road), July 1953
suggested_refs: Street scenes of armed miners in La Paz, 1953
sources: Ernesto Guevara, Otra vez (Back on the Road)
Jon Lee Anderson, Che Guevara: A Revolutionary Life

stops.name: Bolsa Negra, the wolfram mine
stops.campa: With Calica he rides out to the state wolfram mine at Bolsa Negra, high under the glaciers of Mururata, to see the revolution where it works. The miners, the same class that stormed La Paz with dynamite, show the visitors the tunnels, the thin air, the short lives. Ernesto descends into the mountain and comes up with the conviction that here, not in the ministries, lives the real force of Bolivia. Thirteen years later he will come back to this country to bet his life on that conviction, and lose it.
suggested_refs: The Bolsa Negra wolfram mine beneath Mururata, Bolivia
sources: Ernesto Guevara, Otra vez (Back on the Road)
Carlos 'Calica' Ferrer, De Ernesto al Che

stops.name: Guayaquil, the swerve toward Guatemala
stops.campa: In the humid river port of Guayaquil, camped in a boarding house with a floating population of Argentine wanderers, the plan dissolves and re-forms. Ricardo Rojo and the others are heading for Guatemala, where Colonel Árbenz is expropriating the United Fruit Company and building something unheard of. Venezuela and the waiting Granado lose the coin toss of history: Ernesto scrapes a free passage and swings north. The canon marks Guayaquil as the hinge: the place where the itinerary of a curious doctor became the trajectory of a revolutionary.
suggested_refs: Ricardo Rojo's memoir Mi amigo el Che, on the Guayaquil decision
sources: Ricardo Rojo, Mi amigo el Che
Jon Lee Anderson, Che Guevara: A Revolutionary Life

stops.name: San José de Costa Rica, the Moncada veterans and the oath before Stalin
stops.campa: Crossing Central America on foot, by boat and banana truck, through Panama and the United Fruit dominions that he studies like enemy terrain, Ernesto reaches San José. In the exile cafés he meets survivors of the assault on the Moncada barracks in Cuba, who tell him of a jailed young lawyer named Fidel Castro; he argues with Rómulo Betancourt and takes the measure of the reformists. From here he writes his aunt Beatriz the letter with the oath: he has seen the octopus, and he has sworn before the image of Stalin not to rest until it is destroyed.
stops.quote: Along the way, I had the opportunity to pass through the dominions of the United Fruit, convincing me once again of just how terrible these capitalist octopuses are. I have sworn before a picture of the old and mourned comrade Stalin that I won't rest until I see these capitalist octopuses annihilated.
stops.quote_source: Letter from Ernesto Guevara to his aunt Beatriz, San José, 10 December 1953
suggested_refs: Letter to Beatriz Guevara Lynch, December 1953
sources: Jon Lee Anderson, Che Guevara: A Revolutionary Life
Ernesto Guevara, Otra vez (Back on the Road)

stops.name: Guatemala City: Hilda, and the school of revolution
stops.campa: He arrives on Christmas Eve into the one country in America where the reform is real: Árbenz's Guatemala, land deeds moving to peasants, United Fruit howling to Washington. Penniless, selling encyclopedias and images of the Lord of Esquipulas, he meets Hilda Gadea, Peruvian APRA exile, economist, reader of Mao, who feeds him, lends him books and debates him into sharper politics. Here, among exiles of every defeated Latin American cause, someone first calls the mate-drinking Argentine 'Che'. The name enters the world in Guatemala, waiting for its bearer to grow into it.
suggested_refs: Hilda Gadea's memoir Ernesto: A Memoir of Che Guevara in Guatemala
sources: Hilda Gadea, Ernesto: A Memoir of Che Guevara
Jon Lee Anderson, Che Guevara: A Revolutionary Life

stops.name: Guatemala City, the fall of Árbenz
stops.campa: The CIA's planes come over the city dropping bombs and leaflets, and Castillo Armas's mercenary column walks in from Honduras. Ernesto runs through the blacked-out streets hauling weapons, urging the government to arm the people and fight; he signs up for the militias that are never mustered. On the twenty-seventh of June Árbenz resigns without a battle, and the young doctor watches a democracy die of moderation. The lesson burns into him permanently: a revolution that will not defend itself with arms is a revolution already lost. Hunted, he takes asylum in the Argentine embassy.
stops.quote: It was all a lot of fun, what with the bombs, speeches and other distractions to break the monotony I was living in.
stops.quote_source: Letter from Ernesto Guevara to his mother, Guatemala, June-July 1954
suggested_refs: CIA operation PBSUCCESS documents, June 1954
Letters from Guatemala to Celia de la Serna
sources: Jon Lee Anderson, Che Guevara: A Revolutionary Life
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Che_Guevara

stops.name: Mexico City, the photographer of the plazas
stops.campa: The defeated of Guatemala wash up in Mexico City, and Ernesto among them, on the twenty-first of September. He survives as a street photographer in the plazas and an allergy researcher at the General Hospital, climbing volcanoes on weekends: again and again he assaults Popocatépetl, asthma against altitude, and calls it training. Hilda arrives; they marry and a daughter, Hildita, is born. Mexico is the antechamber: the city of Trotsky's tomb now hosts, in its cheap apartments, the future general staff of the Cuban Revolution, not yet assembled.
suggested_refs: Photographs taken by Guevara as a street photographer in Mexico City, 1954-55
sources: Jon Lee Anderson, Che Guevara: A Revolutionary Life
Paco Ignacio Taibo II, Ernesto Guevara, también conocido como el Che

stops.name: Mexico City, Calle Emparan 49, the night with Fidel
stops.campa: In July 1955 Raúl Castro brings his newly amnestied brother to the apartment of María Antonia González at Emparan 49, and Ernesto Guevara meets Fidel Castro. They talk from evening until dawn of Cuba, America, the coming expedition against Batista, and by sunrise the Argentine doctor is enrolled as the invasion's physician, the third confirmed member after the brothers themselves. The diary records the encounter with cool astonishment. The canon records it as the conjunction: the strategist and the prophet of the deed have found each other, ten hours of talk sealing twelve years of war.
stops.quote: A political event is having met Fidel Castro, the Cuban revolutionary, a young, intelligent guy, very sure of himself and extraordinarily audacious; I think we hit it off well.
stops.quote_source: Ernesto Guevara, Mexico diary entry, July 1955
suggested_refs: The apartment at Calle Emparan 49, Colonia Tabacalera, Mexico City
sources: Jon Lee Anderson, Che Guevara: A Revolutionary Life
Paco Ignacio Taibo II, Ernesto Guevara, también conocido como el Che

stops.name: Rancho San Miguel, Chalco, the guerrilla academy
stops.campa: On a dusty ranch outside Chalco, the Spanish Civil War veteran Colonel Alberto Bayo drills Fidel's eighty-odd recruits in marksmanship, night marches and the theory of the guerrilla. The asthmatic Argentine outmarches, outshoots and outstudies the Cubans; Bayo names him the best student of the class, and Fidel promotes him from doctor to soldier. On the crags of Iztaccíhuatl and in the ranch's dry hills, the man now called Che completes the transformation begun at Valparaíso and Baquedano: the stethoscope will board the boat, but next to a rifle.
suggested_refs: Colonel Alberto Bayo's evaluation of Guevara as his best pupil, in Bayo's memoir Mi aporte a la revolución cubana
sources: Alberto Bayo, Mi aporte a la revolución cubana
Jon Lee Anderson, Che Guevara: A Revolutionary Life

stops.name: Mexico City, Miguel Schultz immigration prison
stops.campa: Mexican police sweep up the conspirators in June; Che, taken with cannon evidence of the plot and an unashamed Marxist tongue, is held in the Miguel Schultz street prison longer than nearly all the others. Fidel, released first, refuses to sail without him, 'I will not abandon you,' and the canon counts the vow among Fidel's debts of honor. From his cell the prisoner writes to his parents the letter of farewell to ordinary life, embracing struggle with the fatalism of a man who has already seen his road to the end.
stops.quote: I am not Christ or a philanthropist... I fight for the things I believe in, with all the weapons at my disposal, and try to leave the other man dead so that I don't get nailed to a cross or any other place.
stops.quote_source: Letter from Ernesto Guevara to his parents, Mexico, July 1956
suggested_refs: Prison photograph of Fidel Castro and Che Guevara in the yard of Miguel Schultz, June-July 1956
sources: Jon Lee Anderson, Che Guevara: A Revolutionary Life
Che Guevara, letters 1956

stops.name: Tuxpan, the embarkation of the eighty-two
stops.campa: At half past one in the morning of the twenty-fifth of November, in rain and a norther that has closed the port, eighty-two men file aboard a white pleasure yacht built for twelve, its name a grandmother's endearment: Granma. Lights out, engines low, she slips down the Tuxpan river past the sleeping harbor watch and out into the heaving Gulf. Che is aboard as troop doctor with his asthma inhalers and a rifle. Fidel has promised Cuba a rising for the last days of November; the sea will decide the punctuality.
suggested_refs: The yacht Granma, preserved in Havana
The Tuxpan riverbank embarkation site, Veracruz
sources: Che Guevara, Reminiscences of the Cuban Revolutionary War
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granma_(yacht)

stops.name: The Gulf and the Caribbean, seven days of the Granma
stops.campa: For seven days the little yacht wallows through heavy seas, bilge pumps failing, eighty-two revolutionaries packed among fuel drums, nearly all of them helplessly seasick. They sing the national anthem as they clear Mexican waters, then fall silent for a week of vomit, thirst and cold spray. Che, doctor of the expedition, can offer almost nothing; he records the crossing with clinical mercy. The landing date passes with the boat still at sea. In Santiago, Frank País's rising flares and dies alone. The Granma arrives late to its own legend, which only deepens it.
stops.quote: The entire boat took on an aspect both ridiculous and tragic: men clutching their stomachs, anguish written on their faces, some with their heads in buckets, others lying immobile in the strangest positions.
stops.quote_source: Che Guevara, Reminiscences of the Cuban Revolutionary War, on the Granma crossing
suggested_refs: The Granma's log and route chart, Tuxpan to Cabo Cruz
sources: Che Guevara, Reminiscences of the Cuban Revolutionary War

stops.name: Playa Las Coloradas, the landing in the swamp
stops.campa: At dawn on the second of December the Granma grounds on a mudbank a mile short of solid Cuba, and the invasion wades ashore through two hours of mangrove swamp, losing weapons, food and boots to the black water. Batista's planes are already hunting. A comrade calls it not a landing but a shipwreck, and the canon keeps the phrase because it is exact. Eighty-two exhausted men stagger onto the soil they have come to set alight, sucking stalks of cane as they flee inland. The Cuban Revolution begins waist-deep, late, and lost.
stops.quote: We reached solid ground, lost, stumbling along like so many shadows or ghosts marching in response to some obscure psychic impulse.
stops.quote_source: Che Guevara, Reminiscences of the Cuban Revolutionary War
suggested_refs: The Granma landing site at Las Coloradas, now a national monument
sources: Che Guevara, Reminiscences of the Cuban Revolutionary War
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granma_(yacht)

stops.name: Alegría de Pío, the baptism of fire and the choice
stops.campa: Three days inland, betrayed by their guide, the column is resting in a cane field at Alegría de Pío when the army opens fire at point-blank range. In the rout, Che sees at his feet a box of ammunition and a box of medicine, too heavy to carry both. He picks up the ammunition. A bullet tears his neck; blood sheets down and he believes himself dying, remembering a Jack London character composing himself to die with dignity in the snow. He lives. The canon fixes this cane field as the sacrament: the doctor dies at Alegría de Pío, and the soldier is born.
stops.quote: This was perhaps the first time I was faced with the dilemma of choosing between my dedication to medicine and my duty as a revolutionary soldier. At my feet were a pack full of medicine and a case of ammunition; together they were too heavy to carry. I chose the ammunition.
stops.quote_source: Che Guevara, Reminiscences of the Cuban Revolutionary War, 'Alegría de Pío'
suggested_refs: The Alegría de Pío battle site monument, Niquero municipality
sources: Che Guevara, Reminiscences of the Cuban Revolutionary War

stops.name: Cinco Palmas, the regathering of the twelve
stops.campa: Scattered survivors crawl for two weeks through thorn scrub and betrayal, comrades captured and shot along the beaches, toward the farm of Ramón 'Mongo' Pérez at Cinco Palmas. Fidel arrives with two men and asks how many rifles they saved; told seven, he declares that now they have won the war, and the canon records the arithmetic of faith without blinking. Che's group comes in days later, ragged, bringing the number of armed men to roughly a dozen. From these twelve-odd rifles under the palms, the tradition counts the rebirth of the Cuban Revolution, apostolic in its numbers.
suggested_refs: The Cinco Palmas reunion site, Media Luna municipality; Fidel's 'ahora sí ganamos la guerra'
sources: Che Guevara, Reminiscences of the Cuban Revolutionary War
Jon Lee Anderson, Che Guevara: A Revolutionary Life

stops.name: La Plata, the first victory
stops.campa: Before dawn on the seventeenth of January the reborn guerrilla attacks the small army barracks at the mouth of the La Plata river and takes it: weapons, ammunition, and the news, more valuable than either, that the Rebel Army exists and can win. Che fights as combatant, no longer merely physician. The rebels burn the barracks, treat the enemy wounded courteously and release their prisoners, founding at the first opportunity the code of war that will distinguish them: the wounded soldier of Batista is a future recruit, never a corpse to be made.
suggested_refs: The reconstructed La Plata barracks battle site, Sierra Maestra coast
sources: Che Guevara, Reminiscences of the Cuban Revolutionary War

stops.name: El Uvero, the coming of age
stops.campa: In open daylight the guerrilla assaults the fortified coastal barracks of El Uvero, eighty rebels against a garrison behind sandbags, and takes it in under three hours of the war's hardest fighting yet. The cost is heavy on both sides. Che the doctor returns for one afternoon: he treats the wounded of both armies, then stays behind with the rebel casualties, guiding them for weeks through the mountains back to the column. The Reminiscences pronounce the verdict the canon repeats: at El Uvero the Rebel Army stopped being fugitives and became a force.
stops.quote: For us this was the victory that marked our coming of age.
stops.quote_source: Che Guevara, Reminiscences of the Cuban Revolutionary War, 'El Uvero'
suggested_refs: El Uvero battle monument on the Santiago-Marea del Portillo coast road
sources: Che Guevara, Reminiscences of the Cuban Revolutionary War

stops.name: Sierra Maestra, the star of the Comandante
stops.campa: When Fidel constitutes a second column, he gives it to the Argentine. In a letter to Frank País being signed by the officers, Che writes 'Captain' after his name and Fidel says: put Comandante. Celia Sánchez pins to his beret the small star of the rank: the star the whole world will later know from a single photograph. He is the first man raised to comandante after Fidel himself: the foreigner, the asthmatic, the one who chose the ammunition box. The vanity of it delights him, and he confesses the delight in writing, which is why the canon trusts him.
stops.quote: The dose of vanity we all carry within made me feel like the proudest man on earth that day.
stops.quote_source: Che Guevara, Reminiscences of the Cuban Revolutionary War, on his promotion to Comandante
suggested_refs: The comandante star and black beret, later immortalized in Korda's photograph
sources: Che Guevara, Reminiscences of the Cuban Revolutionary War
Jon Lee Anderson, Che Guevara: A Revolutionary Life

stops.name: El Hombrito, the guerrilla republic
stops.campa: In the valley of El Hombrito, Che's column stops running and starts building: a bread oven, an armory, a shoe workshop, a pig farm, a crude hospital, and a mimeographed newspaper, El Cubano Libre, reviving the name the mambises used against Spain. A tiny hydroelectric dynamo lights the camp. It is the first liberated territory administered by the Revolution, a state the size of a hamlet, run by a man who is discovering that he loves to govern the way he loves to fight: totally, insomniacally, and with a book always open beside the work.
suggested_refs: Surviving copies of El Cubano Libre printed at El Hombrito, 1957
sources: Che Guevara, Reminiscences of the Cuban Revolutionary War
Paco Ignacio Taibo II, Ernesto Guevara, también conocido como el Che

segments.name: The Invasion: Las Villas and Santa Clara

stops.name: El Jíbaro, Column 8 'Ciro Redondo' marches west
stops.campa: Batista's great summer offensive has broken against the Sierra, and Fidel answers with the war's boldest order: two columns will leave the mountains and invade the west, repeating the crossing of the mambí generals Gómez and Maceo in 1895. On the last day of August, Che leads the hundred and forty-odd men of Column 8 'Ciro Redondo' out of El Jíbaro toward Las Villas, five hundred kilometers away across open, garrisoned plain. Camilo Cienfuegos is already ahead of him. The trucks are lost to a storm almost at once; the invasion will walk.
suggested_refs: Fidel Castro's order of 21 August 1958 creating Column 8 and naming Guevara its chief
sources: Che Guevara, Reminiscences of the Cuban Revolutionary War
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Che_Guevara

stops.name: The Camagüey plain, the march of hunger and hurricanes
stops.campa: For six weeks the column crosses the flat cattle country of Camagüey in the middle of hurricane season: swamps to the waist, cyclone rains, nothing to eat but raw horse and unsalted meat, feet rotting in ruined boots, the army and the air force pressing every crossing of road and rail. Ambushed at La Federal and again at Cuatro Compañeros, hunted by planes, the men march by night like a procession of mud statues. Che, asthma raging, marches at the head. The canon ranks these weeks with the worst of the whole war: the invasion's forty days in the wilderness.
suggested_refs: Che's October 1958 report to Fidel on the crossing of Camagüey
sources: Che Guevara, Reminiscences of the Cuban Revolutionary War
Paco Ignacio Taibo II, Ernesto Guevara, también conocido como el Che

stops.name: El Pedrero, Escambray, arrival and the mountain pacts
stops.campa: Gaunt as castaways, Column 8 climbs at last into the Escambray mountains of Las Villas, and Che sets up headquarters at the hamlet of El Pedrero. The sierra is crowded with rival guerrillas, the Directorio, the Segundo Frente, feuding chieftains; and the newcomer does with politics what he does with terrain: he unifies it. The Pedrero Pact binds the Directorio's fighters to the Rebel Army for the coming offensive. Here too a young clandestine courier named Aleida March walks into the camp with money taped to her body, and into the rest of his life.

stops.name: Fomento, the first town falls
stops.campa: The December offensive opens: while Batista's elections die of emptiness, Che's column comes down from the Escambray and besieges Fomento, first town of the plan to cut the island in two. After two days the garrison of over a hundred surrenders: the first town liberated in Las Villas, delirious crowds in the streets, rifles passing from the defeated to the barbudos. The method is now doctrine: surround, cut the roads, take the town, free the prisoners, roll to the next junction. The Central Highway, spine of Cuba, lies just ahead.
suggested_refs: Photographs of Column 8 entering Fomento, 18 December 1958
sources: Che Guevara, Reminiscences of the Cuban Revolutionary War
Paco Ignacio Taibo II, Ernesto Guevara, también conocido como el Che

stops.name: Cabaiguán, the fall from the roof
stops.campa: Guayos and Cabaiguán fall in quick succession as the column reaches the Central Highway itself. Scrambling across a rooftop during the street fighting in Cabaiguán, Che falls from a wall and fractures his left arm; a doctor sets it and the comandante finishes the campaign with his arm in a cast slung in black cloth: the wound the photographs of Santa Clara will show. Six hundred prisoners have been taken in days. He jokes that he is more dangerous to himself than the enemy is. The advance does not pause even one hour for the bones of its commander.
suggested_refs: Photographs of Che at Santa Clara with his fractured arm in a sling, late December 1958
sources: Paco Ignacio Taibo II, Ernesto Guevara, también conocido como el Che
Jon Lee Anderson, Che Guevara: A Revolutionary Life

stops.name: Placetas, the island cut in two
stops.campa: Placetas surrenders in a single day, taken with the Directorio fighters at his side; then Remedios and the port of Caibarién on Christmas Eve, and Camajuaní without a shot. In one week a few hundred men have taken a province's worth of towns from an army with tanks, planes and a US ambassador. Cuba is effectively severed at its waist: nothing moves from Havana to the east except by Che's leave. The soldiers of the dictatorship begin surrendering to the legend as much as to the rifles. One city remains: the provincial capital, Santa Clara.
suggested_refs: Column 8 operational map of the Las Villas campaign, December 1958
sources: Che Guevara, Reminiscences of the Cuban Revolutionary War
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Santa_Clara

stops.name: Santa Clara, Loma del Capiro and the armored train
stops.campa: With some three hundred forty men against three thousand, Che attacks Santa Clara on the twenty-eighth. From the Capiro hill the defenders' great weapon, an armored train packed with four hundred soldiers, cannon and crates of munitions, retreats toward the depot. Che has already sent the university's bulldozer to tear up the rails. The train derails in a shriek of steel; rebels swarm it with rifles and Molotovs, and the oven-hot cars surrender in minutes. The dictatorship's arsenal passes whole to the Revolution, and the canon receives its perfect emblem: the tractor that defeated the train.
suggested_refs: The derailed armored train, preserved as the Monumento a la Toma del Tren Blindado, Santa Clara

stops.name: Santa Clara, surrender of the Leoncio Vidal garrison
stops.campa: House by house, with snipers on the roofs and boys running ammunition, the city falls through the last days of the year: the police station, the Grand Hotel, the barracks one by one. In the night of the thirty-first, Batista puts his family and his gold on a plane and flees Cuba. On New Year's Day the Leoncio Vidal regiment, the largest garrison in central Cuba, surrenders to Che without a final assault. The Battle of Santa Clara is the crown of the war; that same night, Fidel's order sends Camilo and Che racing down the empty highway to Havana.

sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Santa_Clara

segments.name: Havana: The Years of the Ministries

stops.name: Havana, La Cabaña fortress
stops.campa: On the third of January, Column 8 rolls into Havana and Che takes command of the colonial fortress of San Carlos de la Cabaña, guarding the harbor mouth. Here the Revolution shows both its faces at once: he founds a school and a cultural society for his soldiers, orders them to study or dig; and he presides over the revolutionary tribunals that try the torturers and chiefs of Batista's police, sending scores to the wall. The canon does not flinch from the paredón: it counts the executions as justice, and Che never once disowned them. Aleida is at his side; Hilda arrives to find the war has remarried him.

stops.name: Hiroshima, the pilgrim of the ruins
stops.campa: Sent around the world as the Revolution's first ambassador, Cairo, Delhi, Jakarta, Tokyo, the capitals of Bandung, Che breaks from his handlers' program in Japan and travels overnight, almost secretly, to Hiroshima. He walks the hypocenter, the hospital, the museum of melted stone and shadow, and lays flowers for the dead of the bomb. He asks his Japanese hosts how they can bear friendship with the power that did this. The canon keeps Hiroshima as the pilgrimage where the Cold War became personal to him: he has now seen the octopus and also its fire.
stops.quote: In order to fight better for peace, one must look upon Hiroshima.
stops.quote_source: Postcard written by Che Guevara from Hiroshima to Aleida March, July 1959

stops.name: Havana: President of the National Bank, the banknotes signed 'Che'
stops.campa: In November the Revolution hands its money to the guerrilla: Che is named President of the National Bank of Cuba. The story the canon loves: Fidel asked the room for a good economist, and Che raised his hand, having heard 'a good communist.' He signs the nation's banknotes with the two mocking letters of his nickname, Che, a signature that devalues money by gesture, announcing that in the new Cuba the peso serves the plan and not the other way round. Bankers in New York study the bill and understand they have lost the island.

stops.name: Havana: La Coubre, and the photograph
stops.campa: The French freighter La Coubre, unloading Belgian munitions at the Havana docks, explodes twice on the fourth of March, killing around a hundred; Che runs to the pier and works as a doctor among the mangled. At the funeral march the next day, while Fidel coins 'Patria o Muerte' over the coffins, Alberto Korda's Leica catches the comandante stepping forward at the platform's edge: one frame, eyes fixed on the distance, the star on the beret. Nobody prints it for years. It sleeps in a drawer, waiting to become the most reproduced photograph on earth: the Heroic Guerrilla.

stops.name: Havana, Ministry of Industries and the new man
stops.campa: Named Minister of Industries, Che runs the economy of an island under embargo the way he ran a column: budgets like campaigns, factories like fronts. He works incessantly, refuses every privilege, returns his ministerial salary bonuses, and spends his Sundays cutting cane and stacking sacks in voluntary labor, the liturgy of the New Man he is writing into essays: socialism must produce not only goods but a transformed human being, moved by moral incentive. The photographs of the minister shirtless in the cane rows are the icons of this gospel of work.

stops.name: New York, the United Nations, December 1964
stops.campa: In olive drab before the General Assembly, Che speaks for Cuba while a bazooka fired from across the East River falls short of the building and a woman with a knife is stopped at the gates. The speech proceeds through its own assassination attempts as through weather. He indicts imperialism from the Congo to Vietnam, defends Cuba's executions without blinking, and declines all repentance. On American television he is courteous, ironic, smoking a cigar. The empire's capital looks at its enemy with fascination, and the canon records the visit as a raid conducted entirely with words.
stops.quote: Executions? Yes, we have executed; we are executing, and we will continue to execute as long as is necessary.
stops.quote_source: Che Guevara, address to the UN General Assembly, 11 December 1964

stops.name: Algiers, the last speech
stops.campa: At the Afro-Asian economic seminar in Algiers, Che delivers the speech from which, the canon says, there was no returning: he accuses the socialist countries themselves, the Soviet patrons of Cuba, of complicity with imperialism when they trade with poor nations at world market prices. The hall is stunned; Moscow is coldly furious; in Havana, Raúl calls it betrayal. When Che lands in Cuba on the fourteenth of March, Fidel meets him at the airport and they disappear into forty hours of conversation. He is never again seen in public in Cuba. The vanishing begins here.
stops.quote: There are no borders in this struggle to the death... a victory for any country against imperialism is our victory, just as any country's defeat is a defeat for all.
stops.quote_source: Che Guevara, speech to the Second Economic Seminar of Afro-Asian Solidarity, Algiers, 24 February 1965

stops.name: Havana, the farewell letter
stops.campa: Before leaving Cuba in secret, Che writes to Fidel the letter that closes the Cuban chapter of his life like a testament: he renounces his rank of comandante, his ministries, his Cuban citizenship, everything legal that binds him to the island, keeping only the bond that cannot be renounced. He leaves nothing material to his wife and children beyond the state's ordinary wage. On the third of October Fidel reads the letter aloud to the world, and Cuba learns that its most famous face has gone to fight on other soil, location undisclosed. The canon calls it the letter of the perfect revolutionary death, written two years early.
stops.quote: Other nations of the world summon my modest efforts... I carry to new battlefields the faith that you taught me, the revolutionary spirit of my people... Hasta la victoria siempre. ¡Patria o Muerte!
stops.quote_source: Che Guevara, farewell letter to Fidel Castro, 1 April 1965, read publicly 3 October 1965

stops.name: Dar es Salaam, the shaved head of Ramón Benítez
stops.campa: The most photographed revolutionary alive crosses half the world unseen: head shaved, beard gone, glasses, a false passport, the comandante erased into a middle-aged functionary. In Dar es Salaam he assembles the advance party of black Cuban volunteers for the war in the Congo, where the heirs of murdered Lumumba hold the eastern mountains. Tanzania's harbor is the door to the African front he has preached since Algiers. He takes the Swahili number-name Tatu: Three. Doctor was One, soldier Two; the third man is the internationalist, and he now exists nowhere on paper.

stops.name: Kibamba, Lake Tanganyika, the crossing to Africa
stops.campa: By night launch across Lake Tanganyika, Tatu lands at the rebel base of Kibamba under the Congolese mountains: the first and only time Che Guevara opens a front in person on a new continent. He finds an army that fires from the hip with eyes closed, commanders absent in the bars of Kigoma, and a magic called dawa painted on the fighters to turn bullets to water; he records the belief without mockery and works within it, drilling, doctoring, teaching. He asks to fight as a simple soldier until merit earns him command. The mountains hold seven months of his life.

stops.name: Front de Force / Bendera, the defeat at the power station
stops.campa: Against his judgment but under orders from the distant rebel leadership, the attack goes in against the fortified hydroelectric garrison at Front de Force-Bendera. It fails bloodily; four Cubans die, and in a dead man's pocket the enemy finds a diary that tells Pretoria, Langley and the world that Cubans are fighting in the Congo. The Simbas blame the failure of the dawa and drift away from the front. Che, sick with fevers and asthma in the wet mountains, writes the post-mortem with his customary refusal of consolation: the revolution cannot be imported into an army that will not fight.

stops.name: Lake Tanganyika, the evacuation, 'the history of a failure'
stops.campa: Mobutu's coup, mercenary columns, gunboats on the lake: the eastern rebellion collapses, and on the night of the twenty-first of November the Cubans are taken off the beach at Kibamba in overloaded boats, Che boarding among the last, arguing to the final hour about staying behind alone. Crossing the black water back to Tanzania he begins, in his head, the merciless book of the campaign. Its first sentence, already composed, will open with defeat declared like a diagnosis. The canon values the Congo above many victories, because here the myth proves it can tell the truth about itself.
stops.quote: This is the history of a failure.
stops.quote_source: Che Guevara, Congo Diary, opening line, written up in Dar es Salaam, late 1965

stops.name: Prague, the ghost year
stops.campa: The man who renounced his citizenships now belongs to no country at all. After months hidden in the upper room of the Cuban embassy in Dar es Salaam, writing the Congo book, receiving Aleida in secret for a stolen honeymoon of exiles, he moves to a safe house outside Prague under Czech winter skies, disguised, restless, studying philosophy and the maps of Bolivia. Fidel writes urging him back to Cuba to prepare the next war properly. The canon calls this the ghost year: the world debates whether Che is dead, while he drills his own resurrection.

stops.name: La Paz, Hotel Copacabana, the bald economist
stops.campa: Adolfo Mena González, balding, bespectacled, middle-aged economist of the Organization of American States, checks into room 504 of the Hotel Copacabana on the Prado of La Paz. In the mirror of the wardrobe he photographs himself, pipe in hand: the famous self-portrait of the disguise. Thirteen years after he watched the half-made Bolivian revolution as a hitchhiking doctor, Che re-enters Bolivia to finish the continent's business: a guerrilla foco to draw the Yankees in and make, as he will write, two, three, many Vietnams. Nobody looks twice at the quiet gentleman by the window.

stops.name: Ñancahuazú, the Casa de Calamina, 'a new stage begins'
stops.campa: By jeep across the altiplano and down into the scrub canyons of the southeast, he reaches the farm bought as a front on the Ñancahuazú river: the tin-roofed Casa de Calamina. That night, by lamplight, he rules a fresh notebook and writes the first entry of the last diary: today begins a new stage. Around him gather the fifty of the ELN: Cuban comandantes of the Sierra, Bolivian miners, the woman Tania come down from her deep cover in La Paz society, Régis Debray the French philosopher, Ciro Bustos the Argentine painter. The canyon country will be their monastery, then their trap.
stops.quote: Today a new stage begins.
stops.quote_source: Che Guevara, The Bolivian Diary, first entry, 7 November 1966

stops.name: The Río Grande, the training march and the first deaths
stops.campa: In February the column leaves camp for a training march meant to last two weeks; the country itself declares war instead. For forty-eight days they hack through canyons and thorn, rivers in flood, rations gone, men eating parrots and palm hearts. At the swollen Río Grande the young Bolivian Benjamín, weak with exhaustion, slips from the rocks and the current takes him, the guerrilla's first death, given not by the army but by the land. Days later the river drowns Carlos at another crossing. Che records the omens exactly, and marches the survivors home to find the camp already betrayed.

stops.name: Ñancahuazú river, the first ambush, 23 March
stops.campa: Deserters have talked; the army comes probing up the canyon. The guerrilla's ambush along the Ñancahuazú kills seven soldiers and takes prisoners, weapons and the army's operational plans in the war's opening minutes. The diary entry begins with the day's plain designation: a day of warlike events. The war has started five months early, with the network unbuilt, Debray and Bustos trapped as guests, and the Bolivian Communist Party withholding its men. Che knows the arithmetic and fights anyway; from this day the column is in continuous motion until the ravine at the end.
stops.quote: A day of warlike events.
stops.quote_source: Che Guevara, The Bolivian Diary, 23 March 1967

stops.name: Iripití, the double ambush, the death of El Rubio
stops.campa: At Iripití on the tenth of April the guerrilla springs the same ambush twice in one day, mauling two army companies, taking scores of prisoners and a harvest of weapons, tactically the campaign's most brilliant day. Its price: Captain Jesús Suárez Gayol, El Rubio, veteran of the Sierra and vice-minister in Havana who left a ministry desk for this canyon, lies dead by the river, shot through the head, his grenade unthrown beside him. The diary honors him as the first Cuban blood in Bolivia. Victory and loss are entered in the same column now, every week.

stops.name: Muyupampa, Debray and Bustos walk out
stops.campa: To free the column of its civilians, Che maneuvers to the town of Muyupampa so that Debray and Bustos can slip out disguised as journalists. They are taken within hours, beaten, and paraded; the world learns from their capture that Che Guevara lives and commands in Bolivia. The Yankees respond in kind: Green Berets arrive to raise a Ranger battalion, and the CIA seconds its Cuban-exile interrogators. Worse, in the maneuvering the column splits from Joaquín's rearguard, seventeen men including Tania, and the two halves of the guerrilla will search for each other through the canyons for four months, never to meet again.

stops.name: On the march near the Río Rosita, the thirty-ninth birthday
stops.campa: Deep in the campaign's wandering middle, no radio contact with Havana, no peasant recruits, asthma returning because the medicines were lost with the caves, Che turns thirty-nine on the trail and marks the day in the diary with one of its rare personal entries, measuring himself against the age when a guerrilla must begin to consider his future. The column eats horse meat and moves. The tone is neither hope nor despair but inventory: he is still whole, still fit for the work. The canon reads the entry as the last calm self-portrait, taken standing, in motion, armed.
stops.quote: I have reached thirty-nine and the age is inexorably approaching when I must consider my future as a guerrilla; for now, I am still 'whole'.

stops.name: Samaipata, the raid on the highway town
stops.campa: In the campaign's boldest stroke, the guerrillas flag down vehicles on the Santa Cruz highway, drive into the garrison town of Samaipata by night, seize the post, empty the pharmacy and the shops before the astonished townspeople, and vanish back into the hills with prisoners taken and released. It is the war's greatest propaganda victory and its emptiest: the pharmacy holds none of the asthma medicine Che now needs to breathe. The army encircles the zone with thousands. The foco is famous across the world's front pages, and utterly alone in its canyons.

stops.name: Vado del Yeso, the annihilation of Joaquín and the death of Tania
stops.campa: A peasant named Honorato Rojas, bought by the army, leads Joaquín's lost rearguard to a ford on the Masicuri where Captain Vargas's soldiers wait in the reeds. As the column wades the Río Grande at dusk, guns high, the volley comes: Joaquín, the veterans, and Tania the guerrillera die in the water, her body carried downstream for days. Che, marching to find them, hears the news on the enemy's radio and refuses it as psychological warfare, until the details harden into fact. The rearguard is erased entire. The diary's September opens with seventeen men left, and the noose visible.

stops.name: Alto Seco, the last sermon
stops.campa: The seventeen climb out of the canyons into the cold hamlet of Alto Seco, fifty mud houses at nineteen hundred meters, and buy food from wary villagers whose mayor has already slipped away to inform. That evening, in the little schoolhouse by lamplight, Inti speaks to the assembled peasants about the revolution while Che, gaunt, watches and adds his words; the audience listens in silence and asks about bread. It is the guerrilla's last address to the people it came for: a sermon in an empty church, recorded in the diary with dry, unsparing affection.

stops.name: La Higuera trail, the ambush of 26 September, 'Defeat'
stops.campa: Descending toward the village of La Higuera, the vanguard walks into an army ambush on the trail from Picacho. Coco Peredo, the guerrilla's Bolivian heart, is killed with Miguel and Julio; the column scatters into the gullies under fire, and deserters begin naming names to the Rangers. That night Che opens the diary entry with a single word: Defeat, written the way he writes everything, as fact to be used. The ring of soldiers around the Vallegrande canyons draws tight. Twelve days of life remain, and the diary does not change its tone by one degree.
stops.quote: Defeat.

stops.name: Quebrada del Yuro, the last battle and the capture
stops.campa: Betrayed by a peasant who saw them enter the ravine, the last seventeen are pinned in the Quebrada del Yuro at midday by the new Ranger battalion. Che fights until a bullet destroys his carbine and another tears his leg; hauled up wounded between two comrades, he is cornered by soldiers whose sergeant nearly fires. The prisoner speaks the sentence the trial-record of the canon preserves: he names himself, and appraises his own worth alive. The night before, his final diary entry had recorded, almost gently, that the eleven-month anniversary passed in a bucolic mood. The diary ends; the Passion begins.
stops.quote: Don't shoot! I am Che Guevara, and I am worth more to you alive than dead.
stops.quote_source: Words at capture, Quebrada del Yuro, 8 October 1967, as recorded in Bolivian soldiers' testimony and the canonical accounts

stops.name: La Higuera, the schoolhouse, 9 October 1967
stops.campa: He lies bound all night on the mud floor of the village schoolhouse beside the bodies of his comrades. To the schoolteacher Julia Cortez, who brings him soup, he observes that in Bolivia teachers earn less than the officials' cars are worth, and that the school's walls need paint. At midday the order comes down from the government by radio: no trial. Sergeant Mario Terán enters with his rifle and hesitates before the calm of the prisoner, who speaks to him the sentence with which the canon closes the life, steadying his own executioner's aim. The burst comes. It is one in the afternoon.
stops.quote: Ponte sereno y apunta bien. Vas a matar a un hombre. — Calm yourself, and aim well. You are going to kill a man.
stops.quote_source: Last words to Mario Terán in the La Higuera schoolhouse, 9 October 1967, as fixed in the canonical accounts

stops.name: Vallegrande, the laundry house of Nuestra Señora de Malta
stops.campa: Lashed to the skid of a helicopter, the body is flown to Vallegrande and laid on the concrete washbasin of the hospital laundry, shirtless, eyes open. For two days the town files past; nuns and washerwomen murmur that he looks like Christ taken down, and snip locks of his hair for relics. Freddy Alborta's photograph fixes the scene forever: the officers pointing like donors in an old master. The hands are cut off for the fingerprint archive; the body vanishes into a secret pit by the airstrip, to sleep thirty years until Cuba brings the bones home to a mausoleum at Santa Clara, city of the armored train.
